title: Paid per enrollee by kind of service: San Francisco against the other large counties
question: For which kinds of service do San Francisco billers take in far more, or far less, Medicaid money per enrolled resident than billers in the other large California counties?
finding: Across all services, billers registered in San Francisco were paid $2,174 per enrolled resident in 2023 against a middle figure of $1,379 for the other 16 counties with 200,000 or more enrollees (1.58 times; rank 1 of 17). By family, San Francisco is at least one and a half times the middle in 7 of 17, led by codes beginning S (6.09 times, $239 against $39; the largest code is mental health crisis intervention, per hour (code S9484)), and at or below two thirds of it in 6, lowest in drugs given by a provider (0.23 times). The single service furthest above the middle is medication training and support, per 15 minutes (code H0034): $73.57 per enrollee against $3.73 (19.8 times). San Francisco's enrollees are not like the other counties': 24% were seniors or people with disabilities in 2023 against a middle of 13%, and 20% were 65 or older against 8%.
how: The county file adds up payments by the county where each billing number is registered, by service code and year. Codes were grouped into families by the letter or number range the code set uses, and each county's total was divided by its average number of certified Medi-Cal enrollees that year. San Francisco is set against the middle (median) of the other 16 counties that averaged 200,000 or more enrollees in 2023: Alameda, Contra Costa, Fresno, Kern, Los Angeles, Monterey, Orange, Riverside, Sacramento, San Bernardino, San Diego, San Joaquin, Santa Clara, Stanislaus, Tulare, Ventura. Family rows need $1 million in San Francisco or the equivalent at the middle rate. Single services need $2 million and a middle figure of at least $1 per enrollee; up to ten at one and a half times the middle or more and eight at two thirds or less are shown, then the five largest services that San Francisco bills and the middle county hardly bills at all, for which no multiple is given. The last column is the share of the San Francisco money billed by City government or the University of California.
limits: This compares where billers are registered, not where patients live or were treated, so a county that hosts a national laboratory or a university medical center is credited with patients from everywhere, and a county whose residents are treated next door looks low. San Francisco hosts both. Its enrollees are older and more often disabled than the other counties' (20% aged 65 or over against 8%; 21% children against 37%), which may raise spending on adult care and lower it on children's services. 88% were in managed care against a middle of 90%, and health plans may report payments differently from the State. Counties bill mental-health and drug or alcohol services under their own numbers (94% of San Francisco's money on those codes in 2023 was billed by City government or the University), so differences there may reflect each county's rates and how much it does in-house. Hospital stays, nursing homes and pharmacy are not in the file, cells under 12 claims are withheld, and 2024 is preliminary. The family names are this project's grouping of the code ranges; the largest code in each family is printed beside it.
